question.prompt: A number \(m\) is randomly selected from the set \[\{11,13,15,17,19\},\] and a number \(n\) is randomly selected from \[\{1999,2000,2001,\ldots,2018\}.\] What is the probability that \(m^n\) has a units digit of \(1?\)

solutions.title: Average the probabilities from units digit cycles
solutions.explanation:
The units digit of a power depends only on the units digit of its base. We can therefore examine the short repeating cycles for each possible \(m\).

There are \(20\) possible exponents, from \(1999\) through \(2018\). Exactly five are divisible by \(4\), namely \(2000,2004,2008,2012,2016\), and exactly ten are even.

For each fixed base:

- Powers of \(11\) always end in \(1\), so the probability is \(1\).
- Powers of \(13\) have units digits \(3,9,7,1\), repeating every four powers. They end in \(1\) exactly when \(n\) is divisible by \(4\), giving probability \(5/20=1/4\).
- Powers of \(15\) always end in \(5\), giving probability \(0\).
- Powers of \(17\) have units digits \(7,9,3,1\), repeating every four powers. Again the probability is \(1/4\).
- Powers of \(19\) alternate between units digits \(9\) and \(1\). They end in \(1\) exactly when \(n\) is even, giving probability \(1/2\).

Since the five bases are equally likely, average these five probabilities:
\[
\frac15\left(1+\frac14+0+\frac14+\frac12\right)
=\boxed{\frac25}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\text{E}\).
